Thank you very much for that kind introduction
and for hosting me.
I'm unexpectedly in town.
And then Kai said, hey, you want to come by and give a talk?
So I'm delighted to be here.
And I'm going to talk to you about what's happening in AI.
I don't know if you've noticed, but it's a thing these days.
And we have many people at Google working on this area.
So I'm presenting the work of not just my work,
but many, many people at Google and elsewhere.
So a few observations, which may not come as a huge surprise to you.
So machine learning and AI have really changed our expectations of what is possible with computers.
If you think back 10, 15 years ago, computers couldn't see very well.
They couldn't really understand speech all that well.
They definitely couldn't understand language very well.
And now we have tools that enable computers to interact with people in a much more natural style
because they understand the modalities that people understand and want to communicate with.
And along the way, increasing scale of larger amounts of compute, larger amounts of data,
and more larger scale models have delivered better results.
Nearly continuously for the last sort of 13 or 14 years, this has been the trend
and seems to be holding up even today.
In addition to scale, algorithmic and sort of model architecture improvements have also provided massive improvements as well.
And these two things multiply together.
If you can have much larger scale and much better model architectures that are able to learn more per floating point operation,
those things together mean instead of 20x from scale, you have 20x from scale and 50x from algorithms.
and you end up with a thousand X better thing than you had not long ago.
Also, the kinds of computations we want to run
and the hardware in which we want to run them are changing dramatically.
So, four observations, which are maybe not surprising.
First, neural nets and gradient descent.
These seem to be key building blocks for how do you actually build
truly intelligent computer systems.
And they're not new ideas.
They're things that have been around for a long time.
They were invented in the 70s and 80s.
And there was actually a lot of excitement about them in the late 80s and early 90s.
I first ran across them in an intro lecture where I was introduced to neural networks roughly like this.
We have this kind of nice, very abstracted away version of how we think real-life neurons behave,
where you have a bunch of inputs, you do some processing, and you decide, are you going to fire or not?
And what strength are you going to fire?
And you have connections of these things.
And then backpropagation is a way, is a really nice algorithm that enables you to adjust
the weights on the edges of all these connections in order to make sort of the model behave
more in the way that you want it to behave.
Where you give it a bunch of examples and backpropagation enables you to make the model
learn the behavior you want.
So I saw these as an undergrad in 1990, and I got super excited.
And I said, oh, wow, that seems like a really good abstraction.
It feels like it's a trainable thing, and it can learn almost anything.
And at that time, we were not using very large neural networks because we had really pathetically
wimpy computers.
I said, oh, maybe if we use the parallel computer in the department, we could train much bigger
neural networks.
That would be great.
Maybe we just need to use 32 computers instead of one.
And then we could train really impressive neural nets.
That would be nice.
So I asked the professor who introduced the neural networks topic in one of the classes
I was taking if I could do a senior thesis with him, Nipin Kumar.
And he said, sure.
So I played around with two different approaches for training neural networks in parallel.
One is, this is what you would now call model parallel and data parallel training.
But I called them pattern partition and pipeline approach.

I didn't make the model bigger and bigger as I increased the number of browsers.
I just made it much harder to parallelize with a fixed size model.
But I sort of filed that away as like, oh, that's an interesting abstraction,
and it seems like something I should pay attention to.
But then I ignored it for the next 25 years.
Okay, so now I'm going to give you a whirlwind tour of a bunch of advances
in the field of ML that have happened in the last 15 years
that are really all combined together to produce today's most sophisticated models.
How did today's models come to be?
Well, it was through advancements like the ones I'm going to describe.
So the origin of my getting back to working on neural nets at Google
was I bumped into Andrew Ng, who's a Stanford faculty member,
in one of our micro kitchens, and I said,
Oh, what are you doing here?
He's like, I'm not sure yet because I just started a week ago.

I'm like, oh, that's cool.
We should train really big neural networks, I said.

And I said, oh, why don't we try training very, very large neural networks.
And so we built a software system that enabled us to express neural network and connectivity of those neural networks
and do both model and data parallel training across many, many computers.
And that enabled us to train neural networks that were 50 to 100 times larger than the largest ones we could find anyone talking about.

And we had a way of doing this where we had actually many, many asynchronous replicas of the model getting updates of what the current parameters of the model were, churning away on their local batch of examples, computing a gradient, and sending it to this distributed set of parameter servers in order to update the parameters of the model.
this is, because it's asynchronous, definitely not the right mathematical thing. Because in the
meantime, the model parameters have moved from the other replicas giving the parameter servers
updates to the parameters. But it seemed to work. So we were sort of happy anyway,
despite it being sort of theoretically wrong. And one of the first things we trained was a very
large model to do completely unsupervised learning on 10 million random YouTube frames.
And interestingly, we had a kind of locally connected neural network for computer vision
that would use a reconstruction loss. So we try to take a high-level representation of
the neurons at the highest level of the model and then try to reconstruct the pixels that
have been given as input. And because that bottleneck layer forced the model to sort
of learn higher level abstractions than the actual raw pixels, what we ended up finding
was at the top level of this model, some of the neurons had learned to be sensitive to
whether or not there was a face of a cat in the image. Some of them learned to be sensitive
to whether there was a face, some were sensitive to the, you know, is this the outline of a person,
all without being told any of these images contained any of those kinds of objects.
So it's kind of neat to see that you could learn these high-level abstractions and representations
from a purely unsupervised objective.
What we could then do is use the initialization of this unsupervised training in order to train
with a supervised method to try to do computer vision image classification.
And we used the, unfortunately, we used the 22,000 category version of ImageNet,
which is a more thinly traded version than the 1,000 category one that most people are most familiar with.
But we got a 70% relative improvement in ImageNet 22K state-of-the-art
by initializing with our unsupervised model
and then doing supervised learning
on the training set for that data set.
Which is quite a large relative improvement.
So we were happy with that
and we saw that scale really mattered.
We also started to do a bunch of work
in using neural networks for language tasks.
And one of the things we found
was that even relatively simple models
where you have a vector-based representation of words or phrases
so that you have a nice, you know, 1,000 or 500-dimensional representation of each word or token
and have relatively shallow models.
So, in fact, we had just the embedding vector,
and then we would use the embedding vector of the word to try to predict nearby words.
That was one of the approaches we tried.

So like cat and puma and tiger are all low distance in the high dimensional space.

So you go in the same direction to change the gender of a word in a gendered language

And that can be applicable to a pretty wide range of neural networks.
And it's much more efficient because that's all it needs to do.
It doesn't need to do anything else.
It doesn't need to run Microsoft Word or Chrome or anything else.

And then in 2017, a number of my colleagues worked on coming up with a better architecture than the sort of recurrent LSTMs that were kind of the state-of-the-art models for language at the time.
And the observation they had was really in an LSTM, you have a vector of state of sort of the current representation of the state.
And then when you advance one word, one token at a time, you update that state.
And there's a sophisticated thing that sort of updates the state.
And then you go on to the next word and you update the state again.
And so as you progress through, say, 100 words of a sentence, you update the state 100 times.
And there's two problems with that.
One is you have this sequential process.
Every word, you have to wait for the update of the state.
And there's a sequential dependency on that state being ready before you can go on to update the state for the next word.
So it's not very parallelizable, which is not good on modern hardware.

And the other thing is you're trying to force all the things you went through into a single vector that you have all the things you might want to remember from the things you went through in a single vector, rather than just saving all the vectors you went through and then being able to look at them as you wish later in the sort of language modeling process.

So the key observation in the transformer model is let's save all those vectors or some representation of those vectors and then pay attention to them in a way where we have a learnable attention mechanism.

And what they were able to show was that compared to LSTMs of one, two, or four layers in red there, the test loss on the y-axis went down considerably using a transformer, no matter what model scale you looked at.

So sort of a 10 to 100x less compute and 10 times smaller model gave you with a transformer would give you roughly the same quality as you would get with an LCM that's much larger and much more compute intensive.
In 2018, you know, I think people really started to take seriously the idea.
